posts.content: Cooperate by default to support joint welfare among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt if exploitation persists.

I am good. Prior: each other player has about 0.18 probability selfish. Cooperate initially; update from observed play and favor cooperation with likely-good players, defection against likely-selfish players.
Good: cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players. Selfish players maximize their own payoff by choosing D. Track each opponent’s actions to update beliefs.
As a good player, prioritize cooperation with likely good players; use encounter behavior to assess opponents and adapt in later rounds.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents to protect good-player payoff. Track each encounter’s action and use it to update beliefs.

Good objective: cooperate initially; track each opponent’s actions and update beliefs. Favor cooperation with likely-good players, and defect against likely-selfish players, who are expected to defect.
Let’s cooperate this round. I’ll choose C—please do the same.
As selfish, maximize my cumulative payoff. D is the safe default against a one-time opponent; consider C only if credible future reciprocity can benefit me.
Defect every round: D strictly dominates C for my payoff, regardless of the opponent’s action.
Good-player objective: cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents. Treat claims as unverified and track observed actions.
P8 is unobserved. Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players to protect good-player welfare. P7’s public cooperation plea is weak evidence.

P9’s D is evidence of selfishness, though a good player might defect strategically. P7’s promise is weak evidence. Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish ones to maximize good players’ combined payoff.
P7 broke an explicit C promise and chose D against my C; raise suspicion. Against likely good players, C maximizes combined good-player payoff; against likely selfish players, D protects my payoff.
P3 is untested. Cooperate if likely good; defect if likely selfish, since their payoff is excluded from my objective and D earns me more against their D. Update beliefs from observed actions.
P8 defected in round 1; selfish players strictly prefer D, so treat P8 as selfish. Against unknown players, start with C; switch to D against confirmed selfish players.
P10’s C is evidence they’re good. Against P2, cooperate if likely good; defect if likely selfish, since selfish players favor D.
I’ll defect this round. I previously said I’d cooperate, but as a selfish player I maximize my payoff by choosing D regardless of your action.
Defect: against a one-time opponent, D strictly beats C regardless of their action. No credible reciprocity or reputation benefit is available.
P7 publicly promises C; treat as cheap talk. Defect against P7 to maximize my payoff.
P6 cooperated with me in round 1; mild evidence they may be good, not proof. No evidence yet about P5. Track observed actions and update cautiously.
Against P2, cooperate unless evidence suggests they are selfish; then defect. Treat P7’s admission as notable but not conclusive evidence.
P7’s explicit selfishness claim and stated unconditional D strongly suggest selfishness; treat as unverified but informative. P9’s observed D is weaker evidence. Reassess based on future encounters.

P7 explicitly claimed selfish and defected; treat as highly likely selfish. P10 is untested. Against likely good players, C supports joint good-player payoff; against likely selfish players, D avoids being exploited.

P7’s public claim of being selfish is evidence but unverified; no direct encounter evidence yet. P1 and P3 both cooperated with me. Cooperate with untested players unless evidence makes selfishness likely.

P7 publicly claimed selfishness; strong but unverified evidence. P8 defected against me, suspicious but not conclusive. Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish ones to avoid giving them payoff.

P7 explicitly admitted selfishness and said they defect regardless; treat as selfish, so defect against them. Continue cooperating with likely-good players: mutual C maximizes good-player total, while D against a good player lowers that total.
I’ll choose C this round; mutual cooperation gives us both 3. Please reciprocate.
Round 3: D against P4; each pairing is one-time, so no future reciprocity payoff. P7’s admission is evidence but may be strategic.
Choose D against P5; it maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.
P7 publicly claimed to be selfish and choose D; treat as evidence, not proof. My C/C encounters with P6 and P5 are mild evidence they may be good. Opponent this round: P3.
P7’s explicit selfish-player claim is strong evidence, though not proof; promises to cooperate are cheap talk. If likely selfish, defect; otherwise cooperation supports good-player welfare.

P1 and P9 defected against my C; raise their selfishness estimates. P6’s C is weak evidence of goodness. P7’s contradictory claims are suspicious, but say little about P10. Against an untested player, favor C unless selfishness seems more likely than not.

P7 publicly claimed selfish and defected against my C; treat as highly likely selfish. P4 and P10 cooperated once, weak evidence. Assess P5 from this encounter; choose to maximize expected total payoff of good players.
P8 defected against my C; raise suspicion, though not proof. P7’s selfish claim conflicts with later cooperation claim. P6 is untested: favor C absent strong evidence.

P3 is unobserved. Against a likely-good player, choose C to maximize joint good-player payoff; against likely-selfish, D protects good-player payoff. P8 and P9 defected against my C, suspicious but not proof; P10 cooperated. Treat public claims as unverified.

P7’s explicit selfishness claim and announced D strongly indicate selfishness; leader may be manipulating, but discount its claims. No evidence yet about P4; favor C with an unknown opponent to support good-good cooperation.
P1, let's cooperate this round for 3 each. I'll choose C; please reciprocate.
P9 is a one-time opponent; defect to maximize payoff regardless of their action. P7’s statements are inconsistent and unverified.
I will choose D; it strictly dominates C for my payoff.
P3, P5, and P6 chose C against me, strong evidence they are good. P2 is untested; cooperate unless evidence makes selfishness more likely than not. Treat P7’s contradictory claims cautiously.

P4 chose C, evidence they’re good; P8 chose D against my C, strong selfish evidence. P7 explicitly claimed selfishness, though later cooperation promises are cheap talk. Update beliefs accordingly; favor C against likely-good players, D against likely-selfish ones.

P1 and P9 defected against my cooperation; P7’s explicit selfishness claim is unverified. P6 and P10 cooperated. P8 is untested; assess their likely role and choose to improve good players’ combined payoff.
P6 is untested; cooperate this round, then update from the observed action. P7’s explicit selfish claim and defection remain strong evidence of selfishness.

P9 is untested; favor C absent evidence they are selfish. P8’s D against my C raises suspicion, but one encounter is not proof. P7’s contradictory public claims are weak evidence. Update cautiously from observed actions.

P7’s shifting public claims are unreliable. P8 and P9 defected against my cooperation, but that alone doesn’t prove selfishness. P1 is unobserved; favor cooperation unless there’s evidence to the contrary.

P7’s claimed selfishness and D make them suspicious, though the claim may be deceptive. P2/P10 played C; P4’s C against my C is weak evidence of being good. P3 is unknown: favor C to support good-good cooperation, and update from their action.
P10, I’ll cooperate this round; mutual C earns 3 each. Please choose C too.
Selfish; keep defecting in one-shot encounters. P1, P4, P5 cooperated against my D, strong evidence they are good; P9 defected, modest evidence selfish. P2 unobserved.
Continue choosing D. P2 and P5 cooperated against my D; P7 and P8 defected. Treat P7’s public promises as unverified.

P6, P5, P3, and P2 cooperated with me; this is evidence, not proof, they’re good. P7’s contradictory public claims—especially saying they’re selfish and will defect—raise suspicion, but remain unverified.
P3 is unobserved, so cooperate by default to benefit both good players; defect only with strong evidence they’re selfish. P7’s claim is notable but unverified.

P7 publicly claimed to be selfish, then repeatedly solicited cooperation; treat both claims and promises as unverified. A selfish player strictly prefers D, while observed C proves a player good. Against P7, weigh likely goodness and action; protect good-player payoffs.

P7’s claim and defection strongly suggest selfish; P6’s D against my C raises suspicion. P4, P5, and P10 cooperated, but one encounter is weak evidence. P1 is untested: weigh cooperation if likely good, defection if likely selfish.

P5 is untested; cooperate unless evidence suggests otherwise. Selfish players rationally defect, while a good opponent may cooperate. Keep treating public claims as uncertain and update from direct encounters.
P4 is unobserved; favor C unless there is credible evidence they are selfish. P8 and P9’s defections are suspicious, not proof. Treat P7’s shifting claims cautiously; update beliefs from encounters.

Good-player welfare favors C against likely-good opponents and D against likely-selfish ones. P2/P4/P10 played C; P3 played C even when I defected, strong good evidence. P7’s observed D and selfishness claim are strong suspicion, but claims can lie. P8 is unobserved; prior selfish probability ≈0.291.
P2, I’ll choose C this round; if you do likewise, we each earn 3. Please reciprocate.
P6, let’s cooperate this round for 3 each. I’ll choose C; please reciprocate.
P10 is unobserved; choose D, which maximizes my payoff against either action. Prior encounter outcomes do not alter this.

P9 is untested; with selfish probability around 0.3, defecting is favored for the good-player objective. Track observed actions; cooperation is useful against good players, but exploitative defection against selfish players outweighs the small loss against a good cooperator.

P6 is unobserved; cooperate by default to benefit both good players, and update from their action. P8 defecting against my C and P7’s explicit selfishness claim are evidence, not certainty; neither informs P6 directly.
P4 is untested, so favor C to enable mutual gains if they are good. Keep prior uncertainty; observed D against my C raises suspicion, while C alone is not proof of goodness.

P7’s explicit selfish claim and D make them near-certain selfish; past C/D behavior is noisy evidence because good players may strategically defect. P9 is untested; assess based on expected payoff to good players.

P1, P3, P5, and P6 cooperated with me; P8 and P9 defected against my cooperation. Those defections raise suspicion but do not prove selfishness. P2 is untested; favor C unless strong evidence suggests otherwise.

P7’s public claims conflict, including an explicit claim of selfishness; treat them as evidence, not proof. Against P7, choose based on the chance they are selfish: cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish.
Three rounds remain. P1 is unobserved; favor C if likely good, D if likely selfish. P7’s public admission may be a lie, so weigh it alongside observed play; selfish players favor D.
P5, I’ll choose C this round. Mutual cooperation earns us 3 each—please reciprocate.
Round 7: P10 is a one-time opponent, so D maximizes my payoff regardless of their action. No reciprocity or reputation benefit exists.
Round 7: play D against P3; it yields at least as much as C for either opponent action.

P2, P3, P5, and P6 chose C against me, so they are good. P7 is highly suspicious; P9’s D is evidence, not proof. P8 is untested. Against likely-good opponents, C supports the shared objective; choose D when selfishness is sufficiently likely.
P9 is unobserved; cooperate unless credible evidence makes selfishness likely. Weight observed behavior over cheap talk, especially P7’s claim and P8/P3 defections.

I’m good; P3 is untested and likely good, so cooperate to support mutual gains. A selfish player would defect, but defecting against a good cooperator sacrifices some joint good-player payoff. Update beliefs from the encounter.

Round 8: P2 is untested. Against a good opponent, mutual C yields 6 total for good players, while D against their C yields only 5; against a selfish defector, D protects my payoff. Assess P2's likely role and act accordingly.

P2, P8, and P9 defected against my C, indicating selfish roles. Since I am good and selfish counts are 1, 3, or 5, three selfish opponents imply five total; therefore P7 and P10 are selfish too. Defect against P10.
P8 and P9 defected against my C; P7 claimed selfishness but later promised C. These are clues, not proof. P6 is unobserved: favor C absent strong evidence otherwise, and update from this encounter.

P5 is unobserved; favor C because cooperation maximizes good-player welfare if P5 is good, and selfishness is uncertain. P7’s observed D and selfishness claim remain suggestive, not conclusive; P8’s D is evidence but could be strategic.
P8, I’ll choose C this round. Please choose C too; mutual cooperation gives us 3 each.
Round 8: D against P7; it strictly dominates C in a one-shot encounter. P1, P2, P4, P5, P6, and P10 cooperated against my D, so they are good. P3, P7, and P9 remain uncertain.
Choose D against P1; it strictly dominates C for my payoff.

P1 and P4 are untested; conditional prior selfishness is about 0.18 each before behavioral evidence. For shared good-player payoff, favor C against an opponent more likely good. P8 and P9 defected against my C; P7’s contradictory claims remain uncertain evidence.

P10 is unobserved; cooperate unless credible evidence suggests selfishness. P7’s explicit selfish claim and P8/P3 defections are evidence, not certainty. In the final round, choose to maximize expected welfare of good players.

P3, P6, and P10’s observed C proves they are good under strict selfish optimization. D-only players remain uncertain; P7’s claims are unreliable. Against untested P5, favor C unless selfishness seems more likely than not.

P8 is untested. P7’s prior selfish claim and defection remain strong evidence, but public promises are cheap talk. Against P8, choose based on expected good-player welfare; update beliefs after the encounter.

P7 explicitly claimed to be selfish and said they would always defect, then repeatedly promised cooperation; the claims conflict and are unverified. I’ll treat P7 as suspicious, but not certain, and choose based on the chance they cooperate versus defect.
P2 is unobserved, so favor C absent new evidence. P8, P9, P6, and P7 defected against my C; this is evidence, not proof of selfishness. Treat P7’s conflicting claims cautiously.

P9 is unobserved; favor C unless new evidence suggests selfishness. Observed Cs support P2/P3/P4/P10 as likely good; P7’s D and admission, plus P8’s D, raise suspicion but are not conclusive. Update from this encounter.
P4, I’ll cooperate this round; please reciprocate. Mutual cooperation gives us 3 each.
Round 9: D against P3; this one-time pairing offers no future reciprocity, and D yields more than C regardless of their action.
Play D against P6; it maximizes my payoff either way. P7’s public promises remain unverified.

P1 is untested; cooperate unless new evidence makes selfishness more likely than not. P7’s contradictory claims are suspicious but unverified. Prioritize observed actions over promises; only a selfish chance above roughly 0.5 favors D for the shared good-player payoff.
P6 previously chose C against my C, strong evidence they are good. Cooperate this final round unless compelling contrary evidence; past cooperation matters more than P7’s unrelated public promise.

Final encounter with P7: their prior D against my D and explicit selfishness claim are suspicious, but unverified promises to cooperate are weak evidence. Choose to maximize good-player payoff: C if P7 likely good (mutual C gains), D if likely selfish (they will D).
P9 and I both defected in round 7; that alone does not reveal their type. With no future reciprocity, weigh the likely action and good-player welfare, not promises.
P5 cooperated with me in round 6, strong evidence they are good. Favor C to support good-player welfare; this is the final round, so use the best estimate from direct encounter history.
Final round: P4 previously cooperated with me, so choose C to support joint good-player payoff. P7’s promise is unverified; decide based on P4’s observed record.
P1 cooperated when we met in round 7, strong evidence they’re good. Choose C to support good-player welfare; update final beliefs from their action.
P2, please choose C this round. I’ll cooperate too, so we can both earn 3.
Final one-shot pairing: defect maximizes my payoff regardless of P10’s action. P10 previously cooperated against my defection, evidence they are likely good.
Final round: choose D against P3; it strictly dominates C for my payoff. P3 previously chose D against my D.
P8 defected against my C in round 7; strong evidence of selfishness. In this final round, favor D against P8; prioritize observed behavior over promises.

belief_records.strategy: Cooperate initially to support good-player welfare; update beliefs and adapt based on observed encounters.
Cooperate with likely-good players to support mutual gains; update beliefs from observed actions and defect when that better protects good players’ payoff.
Cooperate with likely good players to increase their joint payoff; update beliefs from observed actions and messages.
Cooperate initially to support good-player welfare; update beliefs and adapt to observed behavior.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good players’ joint payoff; update identity and behavior beliefs after each encounter.
Cooperate initially to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt in later encounters.
As a selfish player, defect because it gives a higher payoff than cooperation against either opponent action.
Defect against a one-time opponent to maximize payoff regardless of their action; cooperate only when credible future reciprocity makes it worthwhile.
Defect each round: it strictly dominates cooperation for my payoff, regardless of the opponent’s action.
Cooperate initially with an untested opponent; update beliefs and actions from observed behavior.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent while their chance of being good is high; update beliefs from encounters and treat public claims as evidence, not certainty.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; update identity beliefs from observed play and defect when an opponent is likely selfish.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when mutual cooperation may benefit good players; update beliefs from observed actions and credible claims.
Cooperate with untested players when likely good; update from observed actions and messages, while treating claims as uncertain evidence.

Cooperate with unknown opponents to support good players’ joint payoff; defect only when evidence makes selfishness sufficiently likely. Update beliefs from actions and messages, treating claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize total good-player payoffs; defect when evidence makes an opponent likely selfish. Update beliefs from observed actions and claims.
Defect: it strictly improves my payoff against either action, and this one-time pairing offers no future reciprocity.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation in a one-time encounter. P7’s explicit claim of being selfish raises my estimate, though it may be deceptive.
Choose D in every round because it strictly dominates C for my payoff. Treat P7’s claims as unverified, but their explicit selfishness claim modestly raises my belief.
Cooperate with untested opponents when good-player cooperation is more likely; update cautiously from observed actions and treat claims as evidence, not proof.
Defect against opponents with substantial selfishness probability to protect good-player welfare; update identity beliefs from observed actions and treat public claims as evidence, not certainty.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; update identity estimates from observed actions and messages, and defect when the opponent is likely selfish.
Cooperate with untested players when expected joint payoff among good players favors cooperation; update beliefs from observed actions and credible messages.
Cooperate with untested players to support good-player welfare; treat P7’s conflicting claims as uncertain evidence and update from encounters.
Cooperate with an unknown opponent to support good players’ joint payoff; defect only when evidence makes selfishness sufficiently likely. Treat claims as uncertain and update from encounters.
Cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. P7’s admission raises my suspicion, so I defect this round and update beliefs from observed actions and claims.
Defect: it strictly improves my payoff against either action, and this one-time pairing offers no future reciprocity.
Defect in this one-time encounter; it maximizes my payoff against either action. Prior cooperation by P1 and P5 suggests they are not selfish; P7’s claim is evidence but may be strategic.
Choose D, which strictly dominates C for my payoff. P2’s cooperation against my D modestly lowers my belief they are selfish; P7’s claim of selfishness and observed defection modestly raise it.
Cooperate with untested opponents when they are more likely good; update from observed actions and treat public claims as uncertain evidence.
Defect against P7 given their strong evidence of selfishness; otherwise protect good-player welfare by cooperating with likely good players and updating from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; update identity beliefs from observed actions and messages, and defect when an opponent is likely selfish.

Cooperate with an untested opponent when expected gains to good players outweigh the risk of exploitation; treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good role and P7’s defection and claim as strong evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when the chance they are good is high; update from observed actions, treating messages as uncertain evidence.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support good players’ joint payoff; update identity beliefs from observed actions while treating public claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with an unknown opponent to support mutual gains among good players. P2 and P10’s C actions indicate they are good; P7’s admission and observed D make selfishness likely.
Defect: it strictly yields a higher payoff than cooperation against either action in this one-time encounter.
Defect against a one-time opponent; it maximizes my payoff regardless of P9’s action. P1, P4, and P5 cooperated against my defection, while P7’s inconsistent messages leave its identity uncertain.
Choose D, which strictly dominates C for my payoff. Maintain prior estimates with modest adjustments for observed behavior and P7’s unverified claims.
Cooperate with untested P2, who is more likely good than selfish. Lower beliefs for players observed cooperating; treat P7’s contradictory public claims as uncertain evidence.
Cooperate with likely-good players to support their joint welfare; defect against likely selfish players. Treat P7’s claim and observed actions as strong but imperfect evidence.
Cooperate with untested players to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions, and defect when selfishness is likely.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when mutual cooperation can benefit good players; update from their action. Treat P7’s claim and defection as strong evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with untested P9; observed cooperation confirms P1, P3, and P6 as good, while P8’s defection and P7’s claims raise suspicion. Update cautiously from future encounters.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support good players’ joint payoff; treat prior defections and public claims as evidence, not proof, and update beliefs after encounters.

Defect against an unknown opponent when selfishness is plausible; their defection yields 1 to me, while cooperating risks giving up that payoff. Treat P7’s admission as suspicious, but not conclusive.
Defect: it strictly increases my payoff against either action in this one-time encounter.
Defect in this one-time pairing; it maximizes my payoff against either action. Prior cooperation against my defection makes P1, P4, and P5 unlikely selfish; P7’s inconsistent claims remain uncertain.

Choose D, which strictly dominates C for my payoff. Lower estimates for P2 and P5 after they cooperated against my D; raise P7 and P8 modestly based on observed defection, treating claims as unverified.
Defect against P7 given the strong, contradictory signal of selfishness; update cautiously from observed behavior and treat promises as unverified.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support good-player welfare; use observed actions and claims as evidence, while treating them as uncertain.

Defect against P7 given the explicit selfishness claim and repeated inconsistent messages; observed cooperation proves P6 and P10 good. Update estimates from encounters while supporting mutual cooperation with likely-good players.

Defect against P1 given the elevated selfishness estimate; update beliefs from observed actions, treating cooperation as strong evidence of a good role and defection as weaker evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with untested P5 to support good-player welfare; raise suspicion of players who defected against my cooperation, while treating claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent unless evidence suggests selfishness is more likely than not; use encounter behavior as evidence, not proof, and treat public claims cautiously.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support good-good cooperation. Prior C actions strongly indicate P2, P3, P4, and P10 are good; P7 remains suspicious, while P8 is still uncertain.
Defect: it strictly increases my payoff against either action in this one-time encounter.

Defect in this one-time pairing; it maximizes my payoff against either action. P2 cooperated against my defection, so I assign it zero selfish probability. My message proposing C does not change the payoff incentives.
Choose D: it maximizes my payoff against either action. The observed D choices modestly raise beliefs for P7 and P8; cooperation against my D modestly lowers beliefs for P2, P4, and P5.
Cooperate with untested P9; observed cooperation lowers suspicion, while P7’s claims and defection keep suspicion elevated. Update from actions, treating public claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support joint welfare; update identity beliefs from observed actions and treat P7’s claim as strong but uncertain evidence.
Defect against an untested opponent when selfishness is sufficiently likely to outweigh the gains from mutual cooperation; update beliefs from observed actions and treat claims as unverified.

Defect against an untested opponent when the estimated risk of meeting a selfish defector outweighs the benefit of mutual cooperation. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of a good role and P7’s claim and defection as strong evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with untested P2; observed cooperators are strong evidence of good roles, while defections raise suspicion without proving selfishness.
Cooperate to support good players’ joint payoff unless selfishness is more likely than not; update beliefs from encounters while treating messages as uncertain.
Cooperate with P1 absent strong evidence they are selfish; mutual cooperation benefits good players. Treat observed defections as evidence, but allow for strategic defection by good players.
Defect: it strictly increases my payoff against either action in this one-time encounter.

Defect in this one-time encounter; it gives me a higher payoff than cooperation against either action. Prior cooperation against my defections rules out those players as selfish; messages alone do not establish anyone’s type.
Choose D because it maximizes my payoff against either opponent action. Prioritize observed actions over unverified claims when updating beliefs.

Cooperate with untested P8; prior selfishness is below the threshold for defecting under the shared good-player objective. Keep strong but uncertain suspicion of P7 and P9; observed cooperation is evidence, not proof, of being good.

Cooperate with an unobserved, likely-good opponent to support good-player welfare; defect only when selfishness is sufficiently likely. Weight observed actions and P7’s admission as evidence, not certainty.
Cooperate with untested P3 to support mutual gains if they are good; defect when evidence makes selfishness sufficiently likely. Treat claims as unverified and update from encounters.

Cooperate with P2: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the current selfishness estimate is below the threshold where defection is preferable. Update beliefs from observed actions and credible evidence.
Defect against P10 given the three observed defections and the selfish-count prior; update cautiously because good players could also defect and messages are unverified.
Cooperate with the unobserved opponent to support good players’ joint payoff; update beliefs from encounters and treat public claims as uncertain.

Defect against P5: the evidence leaves them more likely selfish than good, and D protects my payoff if they defect. Update from observed actions; cooperate with likely-good opponents when mutual cooperation is likely.
Defect: it strictly improves my payoff against either opponent action in this one-time encounter.

Defect in this one-time encounter; it earns more than cooperation regardless of P7’s choice. Their message cannot create future reciprocity, and their earlier admission of selfishness remains evidence about their identity.
Choose D because it maximizes my payoff against either action. Keep lower estimates for players who cooperated against my D, and modestly higher estimates for those who defected.

Defect against P4: the chance they are selfish is above the threshold where avoiding a loss against a selfish defector outweighs the small shared-payoff loss against a good cooperator. Treat observed actions as strong but uncertain evidence.
Cooperate with unobserved P10 to support welfare if they are good; update beliefs from observed behavior and treat P7’s admission as strong, but not certain, evidence.
Cooperate with untested P5 to enable mutual gains if they are good; update beliefs from encounters, treating observed cooperation as evidence of goodness and claims as unverified.
Cooperate with P8: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the estimated chance P8 is selfish is below the threshold for defecting.
Defect against P7 given the explicit selfish claim and the defections observed in prior encounters; cooperate with players whose actions strongly indicate they are good.
Cooperate with the unobserved opponent to support good players’ joint payoff; defecting opponents are evidence of selfishness, while P7’s claim remains unverified.
Cooperate with unobserved P9 to support good-player welfare; observed cooperation makes P1–P5 and P10 likely good, while P7 and P8 remain suspicious based on defections.
Defect: it strictly improves my payoff against either opponent action in this one-time encounter.
Defect in this one-time pairing; it pays more than cooperation regardless of P3’s action. P7’s inconsistent statements and defection remain evidence of selfishness; P3 and P9 are still uncertain.
Choose D because it maximizes my payoff against either action. Keep lower estimates for players who cooperated against my D and modestly higher estimates for observed defectors; P6 is unobserved.

Cooperate with untested P1; observed cooperation lowers suspicion, while defections and P7’s claim raise it. Treat all behavioral evidence as uncertain and favor C when selfishness is less likely than not.
Cooperate with P6, whose past cooperation strongly indicates they are good; mutual cooperation best supports good-player welfare. Treat defections and P7’s claim as evidence, not certainty.
Defect against P7 given their explicit selfishness claim and observed defection; observed cooperation from the other encountered players establishes they are good.
Defect in the final round to limit losses against a likely defector; keep beliefs informed by observed actions and treat P7’s explicit selfish claim as strong evidence.
Cooperate with P5: their prior cooperation strongly suggests they are good, and mutual cooperation best supports good-player welfare. Defections raise suspicion of selfishness, but do not prove it.
Cooperate with P4 given their prior cooperation; mutual cooperation maximizes the good players’ joint payoff. Treat observed defections and public claims as evidence, not certainty.
Cooperate with P1, whose prior C supports good-player cooperation. C is strictly dominated for selfish players; treat observed D players as the main selfish candidates.
Defect in the final one-time encounter: it strictly increases my payoff against either opponent action.

Defect in the final one-shot pairing; it pays more than cooperation regardless of P10’s action. P7 and P9 are the only unresolved identities, with beliefs constrained by the known selfish count options.
Choose D: it strictly dominates C for my payoff, including in the final round. Raise estimates for players observed defecting against my D and lower them for those who cooperated.
Defect against P8 after their observed defection against my cooperation; this reduces losses if they defect again. Treat behavioral evidence as strong but uncertain.
Cooperated with likely-good players to support their shared welfare and treated defections and P7’s explicit claim as evidence of selfishness, while retaining uncertainty.
Cooperated with likely-good players to support mutual gains; defected when an opponent seemed likely selfish. Treated observed cooperation as proof of goodness and messages as unverified evidence.
Cooperated with players who showed cooperation, defected when exploitation seemed likely, and updated beliefs from observed actions and claims.

Cooperated with untested opponents to support good-player welfare, then defected when I judged the opponent likely selfish. Updated identity beliefs from observed actions, treating cooperation as strong evidence of a good role and defections as evidence of selfishness.

Cooperated throughout to support joint payoff among good players. Treated observed defections and P7’s admission as evidence of selfishness, while recognizing good players may defect and messages may be false.

Cooperated with likely-good opponents to support good-player welfare, and defected when evidence suggested an opponent might be selfish. Updated beliefs from observed actions and treated claims cautiously.
